title: Air India Pilot Confirmed Positive for Marijuana as Crew Reveals Erratic Cockpit Behavior
excerpt: The captain of the Phuket-Delhi flight that dropped 300 feet could not walk properly after landing and tried to smoke in the cockpit, cabin crew told the airline in a formal complaint.
body:
• The pilot-in-command of Air India flight AI 2379 failed his confirmatory drug test and was found to have consumed marijuana before the Phuket-Delhi flight.
  • Cabin crew filed a formal complaint alleging the pilot sat on the cockpit floor, attempted to smoke, and could not walk properly after landing.
  • The young co-pilot single-handedly stabilized the Airbus A320 after it momentarily went into a "negative G" situation and landed it safely at Delhi.
  • India's civil aviation ministry summoned outgoing Air India CEO Campbell Wilson, while the DGCA moves to tighten drug testing rules for pilots.

The pilot who was at the controls of Air India's Phuket-Delhi flight when it dropped roughly 300 feet mid-air last Tuesday has failed his confirmatory drug test, with results showing he had consumed marijuana, according to a Times of India report citing multiple sources. The confirmation has deepened what was already one of Indian aviation's most alarming safety investigations in recent years.

More damaging than the test result itself are the accounts now emerging from inside the cockpit. Cabin crew members of flight AI 2379 have filed a formal complaint with Air India describing the captain's behavior as that of someone clearly impaired.

"He was often sitting on the floor of the flight deck and tried to smoke out. Cabin crew had to help him back to his seat. He was not in full control of himself. He was unable to walk properly after exiting the aircraft."

— Source familiar with the investigation, via Times of India

What Happened on Board

The incident occurred on a Phuket-Delhi service operated by an Airbus A320. Multiple sources told the Times of India that the pilot-in-command was acting under the influence of psychoactive substances throughout the flight. When the aircraft experienced its sudden loss of altitude, the captain was reportedly standing and leaning behind the co-pilot's seat rather than in his own.

https://x.com/ndtv/status/2087238590288085334

The Airbus momentarily entered a "negative G" situation — a condition where occupants and unsecured objects briefly float upward due to a sudden downward acceleration. Passengers not wearing seat belts were thrown from their seats, and 20 passengers and four cabin crew members sustained injuries.

The young co-pilot was left to single-handedly stabilize the aircraft and land it safely in Delhi. The co-pilot may have alerted the airline's ground control about the captain's behavior during the flight, which prompted the unusual step of ordering drug tests for the cockpit crew upon landing — rather than the standard breath analyzer test for alcohol.

Government Response

An alarmed civil aviation ministry summoned Air India's outgoing CEO Campbell Wilson to express concern and review the airline's plan for addressing the incident. The meeting also examined how Air India intends to emerge from what the ministry characterized as a "prolonged period of operational turbulence."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=3GTLDF66IYA

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation is now reviewing its rules on "procedure for examination of aviation personnel for consumption of psychoactive substances." Under current DGCA rules, a pilot who tests positive must undergo de-addiction treatment and can only resume flying after being certified drug-free. The pilot also faces potential criminal action beyond aviation regulations.

The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau said in a statement that it is conducting a "systematic collection, preservation and examination of all relevant technical, operational, medical and human-factor evidence" and asked the public to "refrain from drawing conclusions" before its findings are released.

Broader Questions for Air India

The incident raises pointed questions about the robustness of India's pre-flight screening systems and Air India's internal safety culture. Senior Indian pilots have pushed for a distinction between testing positive after taking prescribed sleeping or anxiety medication — which can trigger false positives — and the consumption of "true" psychoactive substances such as marijuana.

For Air India, the timing is particularly damaging. The Tata Group-owned carrier, backed by partner Singapore Airlines, has invested heavily in fleet renewal and cosmetic improvements as it tries to rebuild public trust following the fatal Ahmedabad crash in June 2025. But the airline continues to face questions about operational leadership and professional culture — the kind of systemic issues that no amount of capital can solve alone.

The AAIB investigation will need to determine whether the aircraft's sudden altitude loss was caused by a series of rare technical malfunctions — as the co-pilot's report suggests — or by the impaired captain's actions. The answer could reshape how Indian regulators approach drug testing and cockpit oversight for years to come.
